blocks.text: A 68-year-old woman slips on ice and lands on her outstretched hand. Her wrist looks like the back of a dinner fork, and an hour later her thumb and index finger are tingling. The bone broke in a typical way, and the neighbouring nerve is in the firing line because of where the fragment ended up.

blocks.markdown: A **fracture** is a break in the continuity of a bone. In clinical practice the useful questions are: which bone, where in the bone, how the fragments are displaced, and which nerves and vessels lie next to the break. Common fractures follow repeatable patterns because the force that causes them (for example a fall on the outstretched hand) is channelled through the same weak points each time.

blocks.title: Fracture healing
blocks.text: Bone heals by a repair process that rebuilds the original tissue rather than forming a scar. The usual sequence is: (1) haematoma and inflammation, (2) soft (fibrocartilaginous) callus, (3) hard (bony) callus, and (4) remodelling. The process takes weeks to months, depending on the bone, the patient's age and blood supply.

rows: Distal radius (Colles)
Fall on outstretched hand with the wrist extended; often older women with reduced bone density
Transverse fracture of the distal radius about 2.5 cm from the wrist, with dorsal displacement and angulation of the distal fragment (dinner fork deformity)
Median nerve compression (acute carpal tunnel syndrome); late rupture of extensor pollicis longus tendon
Distal radius (Smith, reverse Colles)
Fall on the back of a flexed hand
Distal fragment displaced towards the palm (volar)
Similar wrist injuries
Clavicle
Fall on the shoulder or outstretched hand

Most often at the junction of the middle and lateral thirds, the weakest point; the medial fragment is pulled up by sternocleidomastoid and the lateral fragment is pulled down by the weight of the arm
Neurovascular injury is uncommon, but the subclavian vessels and brachial plexus lie behind the middle of the clavicle

blocks.markdown: **Colles fracture.** In a fall on the outstretched hand the force passes through the hand to the radius. The distal fragment is driven backwards (dorsally), producing the 'dinner fork' deformity. The median nerve passes through the carpal tunnel immediately in front of the distal radius and can be compressed by haematoma and swelling, giving tingling of the lateral three and a half digits. The tendon of extensor pollicis longus winds around Lister's tubercle on the distal radius and can rupture later.

blocks.title: Explaining the clavicle fracture
blocks.prompt: Why does a clavicular fracture at the junction of the middle and lateral thirds typically leave the medial fragment elevated and the lateral fragment depressed?

steps.text: The medial fragment remains attached to the sternocleidomastoid, which pulls it upward and backward.
The lateral fragment is attached to the acromion and supports the weight of the arm through the coracoclavicular ligaments, so the weight of the arm pulls it down.
The two forces move the fragments in opposite directions, producing the typical step deformity.

blocks.answer: The medial fragment is lifted by sternocleidomastoid; the lateral fragment is dragged down by the weight of the arm.

blocks.title: Relating a fracture site to its neurovascular complication
blocks.text: Nerves and vessels lie against bone at predictable sites. The axillary nerve winds round the surgical neck of the humerus; the radial nerve lies in the spiral groove of the humeral shaft; the brachial artery and median nerve lie in front of the supracondylar region of the humerus; the ulnar nerve passes behind the medial epicondyle; the common fibular nerve winds round the neck of the fibula; and the popliteal artery lies against the posterior knee. The fracture site therefore predicts the injury.

blocks.title: Predicting the complication
blocks.prompt: A 7-year-old falls from a climbing frame and has a displaced supracondylar fracture of the humerus. The hand is pale and the radial pulse is weak. What structure is injured, and why?

steps.text: At the supracondylar level the brachial artery runs in front of the humerus, close to the bone.
The sharp proximal fragment can kink or tear the artery.
A weak pulse and pale hand indicate reduced blood flow in the brachial artery, which is a surgical emergency.

blocks.answer: The brachial artery (and possibly the median nerve) is injured by the fracture fragments.

blocks.markdown: **Stages of fracture healing.** In the first hours to days a **haematoma** forms around the fracture from torn blood vessels, and inflammatory cells clean the site. Over about one to three weeks, new blood vessels and fibroblasts form a **soft callus** of fibrous tissue and cartilage that bridges the gap. This is gradually replaced by a **hard callus** of woven bone, over weeks to a few months, which stabilises the fracture. Finally, over months to years, **remodelling** replaces woven bone with lamellar bone and reshapes the bone according to the stresses on it. The timing varies, and these intervals are approximate.

blocks.title: Healing needs blood supply
blocks.text: A fracture that disrupts the blood supply of a bone fragment (for example intracapsular femoral neck or scaphoid waist fractures) can fail to heal and lead to avascular necrosis or non-union. Always consider the blood supply when judging a fracture.

points: Common patterns: Colles fracture of the distal radius (dorsal displacement), clavicle fracture at the junction of the middle and lateral thirds, and intracapsular fracture of the neck of the femur.

A fracture site predicts its neurovascular complication, for example surgical neck of humerus with the axillary nerve, midshaft humerus with the radial nerve, supracondylar fracture with the brachial artery and median nerve.
Fracture healing proceeds through haematoma, soft callus, hard callus and remodelling.

questions.stem: In a Colles fracture of the distal radius, in which direction is the distal fragment displaced?

distractorRationale.b: Volar displacement occurs in a Smith fracture.
distractorRationale.c: Medial displacement is not the typical pattern.

questions.explanation: In a Colles fracture the distal fragment is displaced and angulated dorsally, producing the dinner fork deformity. It typically follows a fall on the outstretched hand with the wrist extended.

questions.stem: At which site is the clavicle most commonly fractured?

options.text: Junction of the middle and lateral thirds
Lateral end near the acromioclavicular joint

questions.correctOptionText: Junction of the middle and lateral thirds

distractorRationale.c: Lateral end fractures are less common.
distractorRationale.d: The conoid tubercle is a ligament attachment, not the usual fracture site.

questions.explanation: The junction of the middle and lateral thirds is the weakest part of the clavicle. Fractures at this site are common after falls on the shoulder or outstretched hand.

questions.stem: After a midclavicular fracture, why is the medial fragment elevated?

options.text: It is pulled upward by sternocleidomastoid
It is pulled upward by the weight of the arm
It is pulled upward by pectoralis minor
It is pushed upward by the first rib

questions.correctOptionText: It is pulled upward by sternocleidomastoid

distractorRationale.b: The weight of the arm pulls the lateral fragment down.
distractorRationale.c: Pectoralis minor attaches to the coracoid process, not the clavicle.
distractorRationale.d: The first rib does not push the clavicle upwards.

questions.explanation: The medial fragment remains attached to the sternocleidomastoid, which pulls it up. The lateral fragment drops because it carries the weight of the arm.

questions.stem: An 82-year-old woman falls and has a shortened, externally rotated leg. A radiograph shows a displaced fracture through the neck of the femur inside the joint capsule. Which complication is she most at risk of?

options.text: Avascular necrosis of the femoral head

questions.correctOptionText: Avascular necrosis of the femoral head

distractorRationale.b: Carpal tunnel syndrome is a wrist problem.
distractorRationale.c: Wrist drop follows radial nerve injury.
distractorRationale.d: The axillary nerve is in the shoulder.

questions.explanation: Displacement of an intracapsular neck fracture tears the retinacular arteries that supply the head. This can leave the head ischaemic and lead to avascular necrosis.

questions.stem: A fracture of the surgical neck of the humerus is most likely to injure which nerve?

distractorRationale.b: The radial nerve is vulnerable in the spiral groove of the shaft.
distractorRationale.c: The ulnar nerve is vulnerable at the medial epicondyle.
distractorRationale.d: The musculocutaneous nerve is not closely related to the surgical neck.

questions.explanation: The axillary nerve winds around the surgical neck of the humerus beneath deltoid, so a fracture here can injure it. The result is weak abduction and numbness over the lower deltoid.

questions.stem: A midshaft fracture of the humerus most commonly injures which nerve, and with what sign?

distractorRationale.b: Median nerve injury causes weak thumb opposition.
distractorRationale.c: Ulnar nerve injury causes claw hand.
distractorRationale.d: The axillary nerve does not cause foot drop.

questions.explanation: The radial nerve lies in the spiral groove on the posterior shaft of the humerus. Injury there paralyses the wrist extensors, causing wrist drop.

questions.stem: What is the first stage of fracture healing?

distractorRationale.d: Soft callus follows the haematoma stage.

questions.explanation: Bleeding from torn vessels forms a haematoma, and inflammatory cells clear debris. The later stages are soft callus, hard callus and remodelling.

questions.stem: True or false: a displaced supracondylar fracture of the humerus in a child can injure the brachial artery.

distractorRationale.b: The brachial artery runs in front of the supracondylar region and can be kinked or torn by the fragments.

questions.explanation: The brachial artery and median nerve lie in front of the distal humerus, so the sharp proximal fragment can injure them. A weak or absent pulse with a pale hand is an emergency.

questions.stem: Describe the typical pattern of a Colles fracture of the distal radius, its usual mechanism, and one nerve complication.
markingGuide: Mechanism: fall on the outstretched hand with the wrist extended; often older women.
Transverse fracture of the distal radius about 2.5 cm from the wrist.
Distal fragment displaced and angulated dorsally (dinner fork deformity).
Median nerve compression in the carpal tunnel (acute carpal tunnel syndrome).
Late complication: rupture of extensor pollicis longus.
questions.explanation: The force travels through the hand to the radius, which breaks at its distal end. The median nerve lies just in front of the distal radius, so it is vulnerable to swelling or displacement.

questions.stem: Describe the stages of fracture healing, and explain why a fracture of the intracapsular neck of the femur may fail to heal.
markingGuide: Soft (fibrocartilaginous) callus (about one to three weeks).
Hard (bony) callus of woven bone (weeks to months).
Remodelling to lamellar bone (months to years).
Intracapsular neck of femur: retinacular arteries torn, so the femoral head loses blood supply.
questions.explanation: Healing needs a blood supply to bring cells and nutrients to the callus. In the intracapsular femoral neck, the supply to the head can be cut off, so healing may fail.
